title: HOTFIXR: Targeted Synthetic Data for Multilingual Weaknesses
hook: A model can answer the same question well in English and badly in Turkish. Rather than routing everything through English, probe the student's weak spots and synthesize data for exactly those.
key_points: Language-specific competency: the same semantic query gets different, sometimes wrong, answers depending on the prompt's language.
Prior fixes both have costs — routing through English limits expressivity; language-balanced training equalizes but lowers overall performance.
HOTFIXR takes a data-centric route: probe the student model for multilingual weaknesses, then generate synthetic data aimed at them.
Reported gains: +6.2% average on in-distribution tasks across three tasks.
It also reduces fine-tuning-induced catastrophic forgetting by 3.7% on out-of-distribution tasks and 7.1% on four unseen languages.
The transferable idea: target the gap you measured, instead of uniformly rebalancing the whole data mix.
content_html: Ask a model the same question in two languages and you can get two different answers, one of them wrong. Agarwal and colleagues call this language-specific competency, and note that prior work attributes it to misaligned internal semantic representations across languages. The two standard remedies each trade something away: route every query through English and you gain performance but lose expressivity in other languages; train on language-balanced data and you equalize across languages while pulling overall performance down.
extra_html:
The approach

HOTFIXR — Hardness Optimized Training data For Improving X-Lingual Reasoning — is a data-generation framework instead of a training-recipe tweak. Models probe a student model to learn where its multilingual competence actually breaks, then generate synthetic training data aimed at those specific weaknesses. The authors evaluate on three in-distribution tasks, three out-of-distribution tasks, and four out-of-distribution languages, reporting a 6.2% average in-distribution improvement, plus reductions in fine-tuning-induced catastrophic forgetting of 3.7% on OOD tasks and 7.1% on OOD languages. Code is promised on acceptance.

Why it matters

The multilingual result is useful on its own, but the generalizable move is the diagnostic loop: measure the student's failures, synthesize against them, and avoid paying for data the model didn't need. That's the same shape as targeted environment or curriculum generation elsewhere in the self-improvement literature.

related.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning LMs with Self-Generated Instructions
related.hook: Instead of paying humans to write instruction data, have the model write its own — bootstrap instructions, inputs, and outputs from its own generations, filter, and fine-tune.

related.title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
related.hook: Let the model write its own step-by-step rationales, keep only the ones that reach the right answer, fine-tune on those, and repeat — reasoning data that bootstraps itself.

related.title: Textbooks Are All You Need (phi-1)
related.hook: Train a 1.3B code model on a few billion tokens of 'textbook quality' data instead of raw web scale, and it scores 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval — data quality standing in for size.

flashcards.back_html: A model performing better or worse purely because of the language of the prompt — the same semantic query yields different, potentially incorrect, answers across languages.

flashcards.prompt: What is the drawback of fixing LSC with language-balanced training data?

choices.text: It equalizes performance across languages but reduces overall performance
It confines the model's expressivity to English
It requires a separate model per language

flashcards.explanation_html: Balancing levels the playing field at the cost of average quality; routing through English is the approach that sacrifices expressivity instead.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'hardness optimized' mean in HOTFIXR's approach?
flashcards.back_html: Data is generated against weaknesses actually probed in the student model, so the synthetic examples concentrate where that model is failing rather than spreading uniformly.
